projects.title: Book-Crossing Community Insight
projects.meta:
End-to-End Data Pipeline, Data Warehousing & Business Intelligence

Tools: Pentaho Data Integration (PDI) · MySQL · Power BI
projects.body:
Project Overview

Book-Crossing Community Insight is a data engineering and business intelligence project that transforms fragmented book, user, and rating datasets into a structured analytical data warehouse and interactive dashboard.

The project addresses data quality issues in the original CSV files, including duplicate records, missing identifiers, and invalid demographic values. The resulting data pipeline enables users to explore book popularity, author engagement, reader demographics, and geographic distribution through Power BI.

Problem Statement

The original dataset consisted of three separate CSV files without enforced relational integrity. Data quality issues could affect the accuracy and reliability of analytical results.

The objective was to build a repeatable ETL pipeline, organize the processed data into a dimensional data warehouse, and make the data accessible for multidimensional analysis.

Approach & Implementation

01 — Data Integration & ETL

Used Pentaho Data Integration to ingest book, user, and rating data into MySQL. The pipeline applies data cleaning, duplicate removal, domain validation, and record matching before loading the analytical data warehouse.

02 — Data Warehouse Design

Designed a three-layer architecture consisting of Raw, Staging, and Data Warehouse layers. The warehouse uses a star schema with one fact table, fact_ratings, and two dimension tables, dim_book and dim_user.

03 — Data Analysis & BI Dashboard

Connected Power BI to the MySQL data warehouse through ODBC. Developed an interactive dashboard with KPI cards, six visualizations, and slicers for age group, publisher, and publication year.

My Contributions

  • Developed the ETL workflow using Pentaho Data Integration.

  • Designed the data warehouse structure and star schema.

  • Worked with MySQL to store, transform, and organize analytical data.

  • Analyzed book ratings, author engagement, reader demographics, and geographic distribution.

  • Developed the Power BI dashboard to communicate findings through interactive visualizations.

  • Prepared project documentation and presentation materials.

Key Results

  • 111,585 validated rating transactions.

  • 496 unique books represented in the selected dataset.

  • 28,909 unique users.

  • 3-layer data architecture: Raw, Staging, and Data Warehouse.

  • 6 visualizations and interactive filters in the Power BI dashboard.

Key Insights

  • Popularity and rating quality differ: books or authors with higher rating volumes are not necessarily those with the highest average explicit ratings.

  • Demographic analysis requires data quality awareness: missing age values affect how reader segments should be interpreted.

  • Rating values need context: a rating of zero represents implicit engagement rather than an explicit quality score, so it should not be interpreted as a negative review.

Limitations & Future Improvements

The project uses a subset of the full Book-Crossing book catalogue, which limits how broadly the findings can be generalized. Future improvements include incremental data loading, expanding the book catalogue, and distinguishing explicit ratings from implicit engagement more clearly in the dashboard.

What I Learned

This project strengthened my understanding of how data quality, ETL workflows, dimensional modeling, and dashboard design work together in an end-to-end analytics solution. It also helped me connect technical data preparation with the business questions that users need to explore.

projects.title: Customer Shopping Behavior Analysis
projects.meta:
Business Intelligence & Data Visualization

Tools: Tableau Desktop 2026.1
Dataset: Customer Shopping Behavior Dataset
Data Volume: 3,900 customer transaction records
Project Type: Project
projects.body:
01. Project Overview & Context

This project explores customer shopping behavior to understand purchasing patterns, product preferences, promotion usage, and customer loyalty. Using Tableau, we developed a set of interactive dashboards to turn transaction data into visual insights that are easier to understand and explore.

The project consists of four dashboards: Executive Summary, Product & Purchasing Behaviour, Promo & Marketing Effectiveness, and Customer Loyalty & CRM Strategy.

View Interactive Tableau Dashboard

02. Problem

Businesses need to understand how customers purchase products and whether marketing promotions are associated with differences in purchasing behavior. However, raw transaction data can be difficult to interpret without a clear visual presentation.

This project focused on several questions:

  • How does average purchase amount differ between customers using promotions and those not using promotions?

  • Which product categories account for the largest share of purchases?

  • How do purchasing patterns vary across customer segments, seasons, and locations?

  • What patterns can be observed in customer loyalty and subscription status?

03. Approach & Implementation

The project used Tableau to explore the dataset and present the results through four connected dashboards.

Data exploration and visualization

I worked on presenting promotion-related metrics and comparisons through visualizations that make differences between customer groups easier to identify.

Dashboard development

The dashboards combined several visualization techniques, including KPI cards, bar charts, heatmaps, line charts, and stacked bar charts. Each visualization was selected based on the type of comparison or pattern being explored.

Interactive exploration

Filters for location, season, and customer segment allow users to explore the data from different perspectives rather than relying on a single static view.

Visual consistency and data storytelling

The dashboard layouts, labels, colors, and navigation were organized to help users move from an overall business summary to more specific questions about products, promotions, and customer loyalty.

04. My Contribution

My main contribution focused on dashboard visualization and presentation.

  • Promo & Marketing Effectiveness: Developed the dashboard to compare purchase amounts between customers using promotions and those not using promotions, alongside other promotion-related metrics.

  • Executive Summary: Created visualizations to support the overview of key shopping patterns.

  • Dashboard Design: Finalized the layout and visual consistency across the dashboards to improve readability and navigation.

  • Presentation: Prepared the project presentation to communicate the visualization choices and key findings.

05. Impact & What I Learned

Impact

  • Turned 3,900 customer transaction records into interactive visualizations that make purchasing patterns easier to explore.

  • Made it easier to compare average purchase amounts between promotion and non-promotion transactions.

  • Presented findings that challenge the assumption that promotions always correspond to higher purchase amounts.

  • Organized four dashboard sections into a connected overview of shopping behavior, product performance, promotion usage, and customer loyalty.

What I Learned

  • Data Visualization: Learned to select chart types based on the question being explored, rather than using the same chart for every metric.

  • Business Intelligence: Gained experience organizing multiple dashboards around different business questions.

  • Data Storytelling: Learned how dashboard structure, labels, and visual consistency help communicate findings more clearly.

  • Analytical Thinking: Learned to interpret comparisons carefully and avoid treating observed differences as proof of cause and effect.

  • Dashboard Design: Improved my ability to organize information so users can understand the overview first and explore details when needed.

projects.title: Isyaratku — AI-Powered Sign Language Learning Platform
projects.meta:
Role: UI/UX Designer · System Analyst · Documentation & Testing
Project Type: Academic Project
Focus Areas: Accessibility, System Design, User Experience, Functional Testing
projects.body:
1. Project Overview & Context

Isyaratku is a web-based sign language learning platform designed to make sign language education more interactive and accessible. The project aims to help bridge communication barriers between deaf and hard-of-hearing individuals and the wider community by providing a centralized learning experience.

The platform combines visual learning materials, quizzes, learning progress monitoring, and community interaction. AI-powered gesture recognition was also proposed as a way to provide more immediate feedback during sign language practice.

The project aligns with SDG 4: Quality Education and SDG 10: Reduced Inequalities, with an emphasis on making learning more accessible and supporting more inclusive communication.

2. Problem Statement

The project was based on several identified challenges:

  • Many people do not understand sign language, creating communication barriers in everyday interactions.

  • Learning materials that rely primarily on static images or videos may provide limited opportunities for interactive practice.

  • Learners may have difficulty tracking their progress and identifying areas that require further practice.

  • A lack of interactive learning experiences can make sign language education less engaging.

These challenges motivated the design of a platform that brings learning materials, assessments, progress tracking, and community features into one web application.

3. Approach & Implementation

A. UI/UX Design

I contributed to the design of the platform's user interface in Figma, with an emphasis on visual clarity, readability, and a consistent learning experience.

The design uses a dark green and warm cream/white color palette. The layout prioritizes visual learning materials and sign language videos while avoiding unnecessary visual clutter.

The documented interface includes:

  • Landing Page & Sign Up: Introduces the platform and supports account registration.

  • Visual Dictionary: Organizes sign language videos by alphabet and categories.

  • Quiz: Presents video-based questions and displays the final score.

  • Progress Dashboard: Displays learning scores, accuracy, streaks, and weekly activity.

  • Community Hub: Allows users to create posts, upload images, and view other users' posts.

  • Settings: Supports basic profile updates.

B. System Analysis & Design

I contributed to the requirements analysis and system design process by helping translate the identified learning challenges into platform features and user flows.

The system was designed around several key functions: account management, access to learning materials, quiz completion, progress monitoring, community interaction, and profile management.

This process helped connect the problem statement to the proposed solution and clarify how users would interact with the application.

C. Functional Testing & Documentation

I contributed to functional testing and project documentation. According to the project report, the application was tested by performing practical scenarios using two different user accounts.

The documented tests covered:

  • User registration and login.

  • Displaying sign language videos in the visual dictionary.

  • Completing quizzes and viewing scores, accuracy, and points.

  • Saving and displaying learning progress on the dashboard.

  • Creating community posts with images and viewing them from another account.

  • Updating profile information through the settings page.

The report records successful results for these tested scenarios. These findings support the functional behavior documented in the report, but they do not establish quantitative AI recognition accuracy.

D. Presentation & Team Coordination

I also contributed to presenting the project and coordinating group activities. My involvement included helping communicate the project's problem statement, proposed features, design decisions, and testing outcomes.

This required connecting the technical and design aspects of the project into a clear explanation of the proposed user experience and system functionality.

4. My Contribution

My primary contributions focused on the design, analysis, validation, and communication aspects of the project.

  • UI/UX Design: Contributed to the interface design in Figma, including visual consistency, readability, and the presentation of learning-related features.

  • Requirements & System Analysis: Helped analyze the problem, identify system needs, and translate them into proposed features and user flows.

  • Testing & Documentation: Contributed to functional testing and documented the application's behavior and testing outcomes.

  • Presentation & Coordination: Helped present the project and coordinate group work to communicate the solution clearly.

My role focused on ensuring that the proposed solution addressed the identified user needs and that the documented application flows could be evaluated through functional testing.

5. Impact & What I Learned

Project Outcomes

The project report documented successful functional testing of the main application flows, including account management, the visual dictionary, quizzes, progress tracking, community posts, and profile settings.

The project also established a design direction for an accessibility-focused learning platform that combines visual learning resources with assessment and progress-monitoring features.

AI-powered gesture recognition was part of the proposed solution. However, quantitative model evaluation was not established by the functional testing results documented in the report.

Key Learnings

  • Translating user problems into system requirements: Learned how to connect an identified problem to concrete application features.

  • Designing for accessibility: Gained experience considering visual clarity, readability, and the needs of users who rely heavily on visual information.

  • Validating application flows: Learned the importance of testing core user scenarios rather than relying only on interface appearance.

  • Communicating system design: Developed experience presenting the relationship between user needs, interface design, system functionality, and testing outcomes.

Overall, Isyaratku strengthened my interest in system analysis, user-centered product development, and designing digital solutions that respond to real user needs.

projects.title: Sigma Coffee — Coffee Ordering & Loyalty App
projects.meta:
Role: UI/UX Designer · System Analyst
Tools: Figma
Project Type: Academic Project
Course: Human and Computer Interaction
projects.body:
1. Project Overview & Context

Sigma Coffee is a coffee ordering application concept designed to bring product discovery, coffee customization, checkout, payment, order tracking, and customer loyalty features into one digital experience.

Developed as part of a Human and Computer Interaction course, the project focused on applying interaction design principles to a multi-step ordering process. The proposed application allows users to explore coffee products, customize their preferences, select payment methods, monitor order status, and manage their loyalty rewards.

My role focused on UI design, user flow and navigation planning, feature analysis, project documentation, and presentation and team coordination.

2. Problem & Design Goals

The project explored how a coffee ordering application could organize multiple customer activities in one interface without making the ordering journey unnecessarily complicated.

Based on the documented features, the main design goals were:

  • Simplify product discovery: Organize coffee products into categories such as Promo, Now!, and All Menu.

  • Support personalization: Allow users to customize drink size, coffee beans, sugar level, ice level, and additional notes.

  • Clarify the transaction journey: Provide a structured flow from order confirmation to payment and order tracking.

  • Support customer engagement: Integrate loyalty memberships, digital stamps, daily check-ins, and reward points.

  • Centralize account management: Allow users to manage profile information, taste preferences, dietary restrictions, notifications, and order history.

These goals represent the design direction documented in the project. They should not be interpreted as user problems validated through interviews or usability research, since those results have not been confirmed.

3. Approach & Implementation

A. Requirements and Feature Analysis

I contributed to analyzing the application's requirements and organizing its features into related functional areas. The proposed application covers authentication, product browsing, product customization, checkout, payment, order tracking, loyalty rewards, and profile settings.

Grouping the features helped establish the scope of the interface and clarify how the different parts of the application fit into the overall customer journey.

B. User Flow & Navigation Design

I contributed to planning the user flow and navigation structure so users could move between the application's main functions.

The core ordering journey was organized around the following sequence:

  1. Access the application and navigate to the home page.

  2. Browse the menu and select a coffee product.

  3. Customize the product and add it to the cart.

  4. Review the order and choose delivery or pick-up.

  5. Select a payment method and proceed through the payment flow.

  6. View the transaction confirmation, invoice, and order status.

The application also includes supporting journeys for account management, order history, and loyalty rewards.

C. UI Design in Figma

I contributed to designing the application screens in Figma, with attention to layout consistency, visual hierarchy, and the presentation of interactive elements.

The documented interface covers:

  • Splash Screen & Onboarding: Introduces the brand, coffee personalization, rewards, and delivery concept.

  • Authentication: Provides login, registration, password recovery, and proposed social login options.

  • Home & Order Menu: Acts as the main navigation point and organizes product discovery.

  • Product Detail: Presents coffee customization options and an Add to Cart action.

  • Checkout & Payment: Displays the order summary, fulfilment choice, and payment options, including QRIS, mobile banking, and e-wallets.

  • Rewards: Presents membership tiers, digital stamp collection, daily check-ins, and Sigma Points.

  • Order Tracking & Invoice: Organizes order status, transaction details, and invoice-related actions.

  • Profile Settings: Groups personal information, preferences, notification settings, privacy options, and order history.

D. Human-Computer Interaction Principles

The project applied interaction design considerations to the structure and presentation of the interface.

  • Consistency: Maintained a dark, minimalist visual direction across the documented screens.

  • Visibility of system status: Included proposed order progress indicators and payment confirmation screens.

  • User control: Provided actions for product customization, delivery or pick-up selection, and account preferences.

  • Feedback: Incorporated proposed success notifications and transaction summaries after payment.

  • Information organization: Grouped related features into recognizable sections, such as ordering, rewards, and profile management.

These points describe design choices visible in the documentation. Their effectiveness would need to be validated through usability evaluation.

4. My Contribution

My primary responsibilities focused on the design and planning of the user experience, as well as the documentation and communication of the project.

  • UI Design: Contributed to designing application screens and organizing interface elements in Figma.

  • User Flow & Navigation: Helped structure the main navigation and the steps involved in the ordering process.

  • Requirements & Feature Analysis: Contributed to identifying and organizing the application's functional requirements.

  • HCI Application: Applied interaction design considerations to layout consistency, navigation, system feedback, and user control.

  • Documentation: Contributed to preparing the project report and documenting the proposed interface and its features.

  • Presentation & Team Coordination: Helped communicate the design concept, feature structure, and project decisions during the group project.

My contribution centered on translating the proposed application features into a structured interface and communicating the design rationale. The project was completed collaboratively, so these responsibilities represent my individual areas of involvement rather than sole ownership of the entire application.

5. Impact & What I Learned

Project Outcomes

The documented outcome was a multi-screen coffee ordering application design covering product discovery, personalization, transactions, order tracking, rewards, and account management.

The project provided a design concept for connecting these functions within one customer journey. However, the available documentation does not establish measured improvements in usability, user satisfaction, ordering efficiency, or business performance.

Key Learnings

  • Turning requirements into interfaces: Learned to organize application features and translate them into screen-level design decisions.

  • Designing end-to-end user journeys: Developed an understanding of how product selection, customization, checkout, payment, and order tracking connect.

  • Applying HCI principles: Practiced considering consistency, visibility, feedback, and user control when designing interfaces.

  • Collaborating on a design project: Gained experience documenting design decisions, coordinating group work, and presenting the proposed solution.

Overall, Sigma Coffee strengthened my foundation in UI/UX design, interaction design, and system-oriented thinking. It also helped me understand that a complete interface should do more than look visually consistent: it should provide a clear and coherent path through the tasks users need to complete.

projects.title: Predicting Which Customers Will Subscribe
projects.meta:
Role: Data Analyst / Machine Learning Project Contributor
Tools: Python, Pandas, Scikit-learn, Google Colab, Matplotlib, Seaborn
Project Type: Customer Analytics & Classification
Dataset: 3,900 customer records
projects.body:
1. Project Overview & Context

This project focused on predicting whether customers would subscribe to a service based on customer shopping behavior and related attributes. Using a classification approach, the project explored how machine learning could help identify potential subscribers and support data-driven customer targeting.

The analysis covered data quality evaluation, exploratory data analysis (EDA), data preprocessing, model comparison, and performance evaluation.

2. Problem Statement

Understanding which customers are more likely to subscribe can help businesses make more informed decisions about customer segmentation and marketing strategies.

However, customer data must be properly prepared and analyzed before it can be used for prediction. The project aimed to develop a classification model that could distinguish subscribers from non-subscribers while evaluating its performance using multiple metrics.

The target variable was Subscription Status, with two classes: subscribers and non-subscribers.

3. Approach & Implementation

A. Data Cleaning and Quality Evaluation

I worked on evaluating data quality by examining the raw, cleaned, and final datasets. This step helped establish a more reliable foundation for the subsequent analysis and modeling process.

B. Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

I explored customer attributes and purchasing behavior using Python, Pandas, Matplotlib, and Seaborn. Visualizations were used to examine patterns in the dataset and understand the distribution of the target variable before building the classification models.

C. Feature Engineering and Preprocessing

I contributed to preparing the dataset for machine learning by applying feature engineering and preprocessing techniques. These steps helped transform the available customer attributes into a suitable input for classification.

The project also considered potential data leakage, which is important when selecting features for a predictive model.

D. Model Comparison and Evaluation

The project compared four classification algorithms:

  • Logistic Regression

  • Random Forest

  • XGBoost

  • Support Vector Machine (SVM)

The modeling process used an 80:20 stratified train-test split and 10-fold cross-validation. Model performance was evaluated using accuracy, F1-score, ROC-AUC, confusion matrices, and classification reports.

Logistic Regression was selected for further hyperparameter tuning.

E. Result Interpretation and Business Recommendations

I contributed to interpreting the evaluation results and considering their potential business implications.

The results highlighted the importance of looking beyond accuracy alone, particularly because subscribers represented approximately 27% of the dataset. Metrics such as subscriber-class F1-score and ROC-AUC provided additional perspectives on the model's performance.

From a business perspective, subscription predictions could potentially support customer segmentation and targeted marketing. However, these applications would require further validation before being used in an actual business environment.

4. My Contribution

My main contributions to the project included:

  • Evaluating data quality and performing data cleaning.

  • Conducting exploratory data analysis and creating visualizations.

  • Performing feature engineering and data preprocessing.

  • Interpreting model evaluation results and identifying potential business implications.

  • Contributing to the project report and presentation.

I used Python and Pandas for data analysis, Scikit-learn for machine learning workflows, Google Colab as the development environment, and Matplotlib and Seaborn for visualization.

5. Results, Limitations & Key Learnings

Results

The tuned Logistic Regression model achieved the following results on the test set:

  • Accuracy: 86.41%

  • Subscriber-class F1-score: 79.92%

  • ROC-AUC: 91.40%

After hyperparameter tuning, ROC-AUC increased from 90.71% to 91.40%. However, accuracy and subscriber-class F1-score decreased slightly. This showed that tuning did not improve every evaluation metric and reinforced the importance of assessing models from multiple perspectives.

Limitations

The results represent performance on the dataset used in this project and do not establish that the model will perform equally well on new customers or real-world business data.

The dataset also contained more non-subscribers than subscribers, making class-specific evaluation important. In addition, further validation would be needed to confirm that all selected features are available at the actual prediction stage and do not introduce data leakage.

The project did not establish that using the model would increase subscription rates, improve campaign effectiveness, or generate additional revenue.

Key Learnings

This project strengthened my understanding of the relationship between data quality, exploratory analysis, feature preparation, and predictive modeling. I also learned that model evaluation involves more than achieving a high accuracy score: the choice of metrics should reflect the prediction objective and the consequences of classification errors.

Most importantly, I gained experience translating analytical results into potential business applications while recognizing the limitations of data-driven predictions.

projects.title: IMDb Movie Review Sentiment Analysis
projects.meta:
Role: Machine Learning Project Contributor
Project Type: Natural Language Processing (NLP) & Text Classification
Tools: Python, Pandas, NumPy, Scikit-learn, NLTK, Matplotlib, Google Colab
Dataset: 50,000 IMDb movie reviews
projects.body:
1. Project Overview & Context

This project focused on classifying IMDb movie reviews into positive or negative sentiment using Natural Language Processing (NLP) and machine learning techniques.

The project explored how text preprocessing and feature extraction could transform unstructured movie reviews into numerical representations that a classification model could analyze. A Multinomial Naive Bayes classifier was then developed to predict the sentiment of movie reviews.

2. Problem Statement

Movie reviews contain valuable information about audience opinions, but manually analyzing a large collection of reviews can be time-consuming.

The objective of this project was to build a sentiment classification model that could automatically identify whether a movie review expressed a positive or negative opinion.

The project also aimed to evaluate the model's classification performance and test its ability to predict sentiment for new review text.

3. Approach & Implementation

A. Data Cleaning and Exploratory Data Analysis

I worked with a dataset containing 50,000 IMDb reviews labeled as either positive or negative.

The initial analysis involved inspecting sample records and visualizing the sentiment distribution. This helped establish an understanding of the dataset before preprocessing and model development.

B. Text Preprocessing

I implemented a text preprocessing function to standardize the reviews and reduce unnecessary text elements. The process included:

  • Converting text to lowercase.

  • Removing HTML tags.

  • Removing punctuation and numerical digits.

  • Removing English stopwords.

  • Applying stemming using NLTK's Snowball Stemmer.

I also compared review lengths before and after preprocessing to examine how the cleaning process affected the text.

C. Feature Extraction with TF-IDF

Since machine learning models require numerical input, I used TfidfVectorizer from Scikit-learn to convert the cleaned reviews into numerical features.

The vectorizer was configured with a maximum of 5,000 features and an n-gram range of (1, 2), allowing the representation to include individual words as well as two-word combinations.

The sentiment labels were encoded as 0 for negative and 1 for positive.

D. Model Development

I trained a Multinomial Naive Bayes classifier using the TF-IDF representations.

The dataset was divided into training and testing sets using an 80:20 split, with stratification to preserve the class distribution. The random state was set to 42 for reproducibility.

E. Model Evaluation and Prediction Testing

I evaluated the model using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and a confusion matrix.

I also implemented a prediction function that accepts new review text, applies the same preprocessing steps, transforms the text into TF-IDF features, and returns a positive or negative sentiment prediction.

For example, the review "This movie was boring and long" received a predicted negative sentiment, with a negative-class probability of approximately 73.50%.

4. My Contribution

My contributions to this project included:

  • Cleaning and inspecting the review dataset.

  • Conducting exploratory data analysis and visualizing sentiment distribution.

  • Implementing text preprocessing and stemming.

  • Applying TF-IDF for text feature extraction.

  • Building the Multinomial Naive Bayes classification model.

  • Evaluating model performance using classification metrics and a confusion matrix.

  • Testing predictions on new movie reviews.

I used Python, Pandas, and NumPy for data handling, NLTK for text processing, Scikit-learn for feature extraction and model development, Matplotlib for visualization, and Google Colab as the development environment.

5. Results & Key Findings

The Multinomial Naive Bayes model achieved 85.53% test accuracy on 10,000 held-out reviews.

The classification report showed the following results:

Metric Negative Positive
Precision 0.87 0.84
Recall 0.84 0.87
F1-score 0.85 0.86

The results indicate that the model was able to classify both sentiment categories with reasonably balanced performance on the test set.

The project also demonstrated how preprocessing, stemming, and TF-IDF feature extraction can be combined in a text classification workflow. The prediction function made it possible to test the trained model with individual review sentences.

6. Limitations & Future Improvements

Although the model achieved 85.53% accuracy, several limitations should be considered.

Potential data leakage during feature extraction: In the notebook, TF-IDF was fitted on the complete dataset before the train-test split. This means vocabulary selection used information from both the training and test reviews. Although the sentiment labels were not used to fit the vocabulary, this is still a form of preprocessing leakage and may make the test evaluation less reliable. A better approach would be to split the data first and fit the vectorizer only on the training set, preferably within a Scikit-learn pipeline.

Limited model comparison: The notebook evaluated one classification algorithm, Multinomial Naive Bayes. Comparing it with other models, such as Logistic Regression or Support Vector Machines, would help determine whether another approach performs better.

Text understanding limitations: The model relies on word-based TF-IDF features and learned word patterns. It may struggle with sarcasm, complex context, negation, slang, or reviews whose meaning depends on subtle language cues.

Generalization: The reported results come from a single train-test split of this dataset. Additional validation on different review sources or unseen real-world data would be needed before making claims about broader performance.

Future improvements could include correcting the feature extraction workflow, comparing multiple classifiers, conducting cross-validation, and testing the model on more diverse movie reviews.

7. Key Learnings

This project strengthened my understanding of how unstructured text can be prepared and transformed into features for machine learning. It also gave me practical experience in building a complete NLP classification workflow, from data exploration and preprocessing to model evaluation and prediction testing.

Most importantly, I learned that a good accuracy score is not enough on its own. The reliability of the evaluation process, the characteristics of the dataset, and the limitations of the model must also be considered when interpreting machine learning results.

projects.title: Battery Rental System – UML & System Analysis
projects.meta:
Role: System Analysis & UML Documentation
Project Type: Project
Tools: Draw.io (diagrams.net), Microsoft Word
Focus Areas: Requirements Analysis, Business Process Modeling, UML
projects.body:
1. Project Overview & Context

The Battery Rental System was a group project focused on analyzing and modeling the processes involved in a battery rental and purchasing service.

The project covered several business processes, including battery rental, purchase, deposit handling, battery returns, and delivery. The main focus was to translate these processes into structured system requirements and UML diagrams that describe the system's expected behavior and structure.

2. Problem Statement

A system that supports multiple battery-related services needs clearly defined processes and requirements. Without proper system analysis, the relationships between activities, system components, and different operational states may be difficult to understand.

This project addressed the need to document the system's business processes and expected functionality before implementation through requirements analysis and UML modeling.

3. Approach & Implementation

A. Requirements Analysis

I contributed to identifying and documenting the system requirements based on the battery rental and purchasing processes.

The analysis covered rental transactions, purchases, deposits, battery returns, and delivery. These requirements provided a foundation for representing the expected system behavior through UML diagrams.

B. Use Case Diagram

I worked on the Use Case Diagram to represent the system's expected functionality and interactions between users and the system.

This diagram helped organize the functional requirements into a clearer overview of the system's scope.

C. Activity Diagram

I developed Activity Diagram documentation to represent the flow of activities within the system's processes.

This modeling approach helped illustrate the sequence of steps involved in relevant battery rental and purchasing operations.

D. Class Diagram

I contributed to the Class Diagram to describe the system's structural design, including its classes and their relationships.

The diagram provided a structured representation of the system's conceptual components.

E. State Transition Diagram

I worked on the State Transition Diagram to represent how an object or process changes from one state to another based on relevant events or conditions.

This helped document state changes within the system's modeled behavior.

F. Documentation

I contributed to preparing the project report using Microsoft Word. The documentation brought together the requirements analysis and UML models to communicate the proposed system design.

Draw.io (diagrams.net) was used to create the diagrams.

4. My Contribution

As part of the group project, my contributions included:

  • Analyzing and documenting system requirements.

  • Creating the Use Case Diagram.

  • Developing Activity Diagrams to represent process flows.

  • Creating the Class Diagram to represent system structure.

  • Developing the State Transition Diagram to document state changes.

  • Preparing the project report and organizing the system analysis documentation.

My primary focus was on system analysis and UML documentation rather than claiming responsibility for software implementation.

5. Key Learnings

This project strengthened my understanding of how business processes can be translated into structured system requirements and UML models.

I gained practical experience in representing system functionality, activity flows, structural relationships, and state transitions. I also learned the importance of consistent documentation in communicating system requirements within a group project.

The experience helped develop my skills in analytical thinking, process modeling, technical documentation, and collaboration—skills that are relevant to system analysis and business analysis roles.

6. Project Scope & Limitations

This case study focuses on requirements analysis and UML modeling. The available project details do not establish whether the system was implemented, deployed, or tested, so no claims are made about operational performance, usability, or business outcomes.
